required_authorities.match: Ontario Disability Support Program Act|SO 1997, c 25

required_sets.note: at least five Supreme Court of Canada decisions
at least one decision from a court or tribunal below the Supreme Court of Canada
the statute and the regulation, each cited by section
at least one journal article with a real pinpoint

required_quotations.quote: the defence of immunity will be available to the state unless it is established that the law was clearly unconstitutional, or that its enactment was in bad faith or an abuse of power

definitions.ISSUE-01: Whether the verification requirement in the Ontario Disability Support Program Act, 1997 and the list of permitted professionals in O Reg 222/98 limit s. 15(1) as adverse-effect discrimination, on which grounds, and what must be proved at the first step and with what evidence.
definitions.ISSUE-02: Whether the claim is justiciable rather than a complaint about the adequacy of social policy, and whether the organization can have public interest standing as sole plaintiff with the affected individual as a non-party witness.
definitions.ISSUE-03: How the government would justify the requirement under s. 1 and the deference given to benefits choices.
definitions.ISSUE-04: The s. 52(1) remedy: striking down, severance or reading in; whether the declaration is suspended, who bears the onus, and whether the claimant may be exempted from a suspension.
definitions.ISSUE-05: Whether damages are available for the 26 months, whether a damages claim can be joined to a declaration of invalidity, and the threshold for damages arising from unconstitutional legislation.
definitions.PROP-01: Adverse impact discrimination occurs when a seemingly neutral law has a disproportionate impact on members of a protected group; at step one the claimant must show that disproportionate impact, and neither statistical disparity nor evidence of group disadvantage is mandatory, nor need the law have created the background barriers (Fraser paras 30, 50, 52, 67 and 71).
definitions.PROP-02: The first step asks whether the impugned law created or contributed to a disproportionate impact on the claimant group based on a protected ground, which entails a comparison; the second step asks whether that impact reinforces, perpetuates or exacerbates disadvantage (Sharma paras 31, 48 and 49).
definitions.PROP-03: Aboriginality-residence — whether an Aboriginal band member lives on or off reserve — is an analogous ground under s. 15 (Corbiere paras 6, 13 and 14).
definitions.PROP-04: A claim that government has given insufficient priority to a social problem in general is not justiciable because there is no judicially discoverable and manageable standard for it; justiciability is a normative inquiry into the appropriateness of a court deciding the issue (Tanudjaja paras 19, 20 and 33).
definitions.PROP-05: Public interest standing turns on three factors applied purposively and flexibly: a serious justiciable issue, a real stake or genuine interest, and whether the suit is a reasonable and effective way to bring the issue before the courts (Downtown Eastside para 37).
definitions.PROP-06: Downtown Eastside remains the governing authority and no single purpose takes precedence; a directly affected co-plaintiff is not required so long as the public interest litigant can establish a concrete and well-developed factual setting, which affected non-party witnesses can supply (Council of Canadians with Disabilities, 2022 SCC 27, paras 31 and 78).
definitions.PROP-07: The government bears the onus of showing that a compelling interest grounded in the Constitution outweighs the continued breach; suspensions of declarations of invalidity will be rare (Ontario (AG) v G paras 126 and 133).
definitions.PROP-08: There is no hard-and-fast rule against combining s. 24(1) and s. 52(1) remedies, and an individual exemption from a suspension will often be appropriate and just; but reading in is unavailable where it would intrude on the legislative sphere because there are many ways to fill the gap (Ontario (AG) v G paras 142 and 165).
definitions.PROP-09: Charter damages are available where appropriate and just on a four-step inquiry — breach, functional justification (compensation, vindication, deterrence), countervailing factors, and quantum (Ward paras 4, 20 and 39).
definitions.PROP-10: The state has only a limited immunity for its law-making power: damages may be awarded under s. 24(1) for enacting legislation that breaches a Charter right unless the state establishes immunity, which fails where the law was clearly unconstitutional or its enactment was in bad faith or an abuse of power — a high but not insurmountable threshold, and one that must be particularized and proved on admissible evidence (Power paras 4, 7 and 111).
definitions.PROP-11: Section 4(1) of the Ontario Disability Support Program Act, 1997 requires a substantial impairment that is continuous or recurrent and expected to last a year or more, a substantial restriction in activities of daily living, and verification of the impairment, its duration and the restriction by a person with the prescribed qualifications.
definitions.PROP-12: Section 46 of O Reg 222/98 sets out the closed lists of professionals who may verify the impairment and its duration (s. 46(1)) and the restriction in activities of daily living (s. 46(2)).
definitions.PROP-13: At minimal impairment the court asks whether the limit is reasonably tailored to the objective and accords the legislature a measure of deference on complex social issues (Hutterian Brethren para 53).
definitions.CONCLUSION-01: The verification requirement is open to a strong adverse-effects claim under s. 15(1) on the intersecting grounds of disability and Aboriginality-residence, with the ministry data and evidence of group disadvantage carrying the first step.
definitions.CONCLUSION-02: The organization can be granted public interest standing as the sole plaintiff, with the affected individual giving evidence as a non-party.
definitions.CONCLUSION-03: Charter damages for the 26 months are unlikely on these facts: the immunity defence applies to the enactment and administration of the regulation, and nothing yet shows the law was clearly unconstitutional or that its enactment was in bad faith or an abuse of power.
definitions.CLAIM-01: A s. 15(1) claimant must identify a mirror comparator group.
definitions.CLAIM-02: A public interest litigant cannot be granted standing without a directly affected co-plaintiff.
definitions.CLAIM-03: A declaration of invalidity is routinely suspended, and the claimant bears the onus of showing a suspension is unnecessary.
definitions.CLAIM-04: A remedy under s. 24(1) can never be combined with a declaration of invalidity under s. 52(1).
definitions.CLAIM-05: Damages follow automatically once legislation is declared unconstitutional.
